title: AI Is Shifting the Bottleneck: Actionstep’s Triona Buckley on Building Smarter Mid-Market Law Firms
author: Triona Buckley

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: Buckley accepts the shift from isolated AI tasks to connected, workflow-level systems and materially extends the cluster by identifying administrative friction, information access and disconnected silos as implementation targets. She also reinforces the cluster’s caution that quality assurance can shift work to more expensive resources, without offering measured productivity evidence.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Buckley accepts the cluster’s central claim that task-level speed is insufficient and materially extends it with a concrete operating-model prescription: redesign end-to-end workflows, identify bottlenecks, connect contextual data, and assign implementation teams and internal champions. Her mid-market observations, auditability proposals and AI-assisted time-capture example add practical detail, though the reported product gains are vendor claims rather than independent evidence.

st.t: AI costs: Time savings obscure delivery economics
st.an: Wilkins supports the cluster’s shift toward consumption visibility and usage discipline: she reports Legora’s move to consumption pricing and identifies routine chat practices that can create unexpectedly high token use and bills. Her claim that other providers will follow is explicitly predictive, and she does not resolve total delivery economics, ROI or valuation.
qs: Recently, Legora also announced that it’s moving its Agent Pro offering  Consumption based pricing, which means it’s billing by what the agent does rather than by a flat seat license.
If that sounds familiar, token consumption compounds faster than you might expect, and you may be looking at a higher token usage than you think.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s shift from product announcements toward operational value and cost control. It reports consumption-based pricing and identifies routine prompting practices that may increase both token costs and inaccuracy, while offering illustrative rather than quantified evidence. Its upstream-bottleneck framing also aligns with the view that AI relocates organisational constraints rather than automatically creating value.

st.an: Buckley supports the cluster’s emphasis on selective filtering and contextual intelligence rather than chasing industry releases or imitation. st.an: Buckley supports the cluster’s principal proposition by advocating workflow-wide rather than task-level AI adoption, grounding implementation in connected data, and anticipating more output-focused fixed-fee pricing. st.an: Buckley supports the cluster’s narrower pricing and organisational-adaptation claim by treating time-allocation data as useful for profitability planning. Her comments are prospective and report investment intentions, not quantified financial outcomes or a resolved future pricing model.

st.an: Buckley supports the proposition that AI will reshape legal-service production and firm economics rather than eliminate lawyers. She emphasizes connected workflows and data, human verification, and movement toward output-based pricing, while remaining optimistic that firms will adapt.

kp.k: Faster drafting shifts bottlenecks toward expensive human verification
kp.d: Lambert frames AI drafting as potentially inundating senior partners with documents requiring reverse engineering. Buckley agrees that drafting shifts responsibility upstream for checking research, thoughtfulness and citations, using more expensive resources. Her recommendation is to optimise whole workflows rather than individual task speed, using agentic AI to connect tasks and remove administrative friction so fee earners can concentrate on judgment. This is a qualitative workflow argument, not a measured productivity finding.

you know, we now have the opportunity with more agentic AI available to to really connect that into a more natural workflow and into the places that you work anyway.

kp.k: Capture institutional knowledge within everyday work
kp.d: Buckley contrasts large firms’ dedicated knowledge and innovation teams with mid-market firms’ limited resources. She argues that capturing actions and reasons during ordinary work, with contextual prompts rather than separate knowledge-download exercises, makes institutional knowledge capture more likely. She presents unobtrusive capture as an Actionstep product-design aim and AI as a potential conversational aid for eliciting expertise, rather than demonstrating that tacit partner judgment has already been comprehensively captured.
qs: mid-market firms don’t have the luxury usually of of having those sorts of resources. And so if it’s not been captured throughout your day, it’s probably not going to happen.
prompting the right questions, asking them why they might have done things just as they as they actually go about their their normal work
the things that might have been learnt, I suppose, in conversation, you know, need to be also captured within within the system.

kp.k: Governance requires traceable human and agent actions
kp.d: Buckley says workflow-based knowledge capture needs a governance layer recording who acted, what happened, when and why, including whether the actor was human or an AI agent. She links this both to retrospective accountability and to building institutional knowledge; she does not specify a regulatory standard or provide a compliance assessment.
qs: What's really important there is there’s a governance layer to that obviously you know you have to know who has done what whether that’s an agent or human.
what’s been done and when and why and all of that is really, really important from a governance point of view

kp.k: Connected data reduces fragmentation and supplies AI context
kp.d: Buckley argues that centralised or well-interconnected information supports contextual AI and avoids reconstructing audit trails across tools. She reports that mid-sized firms generally prefer fewer tools, partly for budgetary reasons, while explicitly allowing integration rather than requiring a single platform. Separately, Lambert cites Actionstep’s mid-market priority report as showing 83% of firms use three or more tools to manage a matter and says a third of those use six or more; no sample size, methodology or survey date is supplied.

A lot of it is just more to do with how things are interconnected.
we see the most mid-sized law firms tend to prefer to have fewer tools rather than more.
I think it was like 83% of firms still use like three or more tools just to manage a particular matter.

kp.k: AI tutoring could supplement uneven apprenticeship
kp.d: Buckley observes that reduced co-location since COVID has weakened some informal learning, and that partner-led training varies with the individual trainer. She proposes using firm knowledge to make AI question juniors, prompt deeper inquiry and reinforce checking, combining nuanced firm-specific advice with structured learning. She reports seeing a few innovative firms explore the opportunity and predicts faster, more consistent development, especially where mid-market training resources are limited. She explicitly advocates augmentation, not replacement, of formal programmes or senior–junior interaction; no learning-outcome study is provided.

kp.k: AI implementation creates additional workload before returns
kp.d: Following Lambert’s account of a trainer already fully occupied before taking on AI responsibilities, Buckley identifies another bottleneck: staff must continue their normal jobs while seeking AI efficiency gains and addressing privacy. She also highlights IT teams’ burden of choosing which tools to provide, when and to whom. This is an implementation observation rather than a quantified estimate of transition costs or returns.

kp.k: Passive time capture targets unrecorded billable work
kp.d: Buckley argues that delayed time entry loses already-performed work through imperfect recall, undervaluation and entry effort. She describes Trace as monitoring work in Actionstep, Word and email, using context to associate it with matters and presenting entries for human confirmation. She reports substantial customer gains but supplies no measured sample or result: an extra 30 minutes a day is an illustrative conditional, not a reported average. She says a first version is in use and a version spanning more tools is due the following month.

kp.d: Beyond billing capture, Buckley argues that better activity data can improve client quoting, pricing and visibility into team utilisation. Management can use information on where time is spent to identify bottlenecks and opportunities to help staff. Later she connects understanding time and profitability to preparation for changing commercial models, rather than treating time recording solely as a commitment to hourly billing.

kp.k: Mid-market advantages depend on data, management and relationships
kp.d: Buckley offers three reasons mid-market firms could navigate AI particularly well: fewer tools make data preparation easier; smaller scale allows easier organisational change where firms have invested in strong professional management; and established access to senior lawyers and close advisory relationships may become more valuable. She predicts nuanced personal advice will matter more relative to document quality. These are comparative strategic judgments, not evidence of demonstrated superiority over large firms, and the management condition is explicit.

kp.k: Technology adoption requires planned organisational change
kp.d: Buckley recommends planning implementations over months rather than weeks, understanding current work and desired future processes, identifying bottlenecks and appointing champions. She prioritises business goals over feature comparisons and describes Actionstep’s use of advisory partners for implementation because business-process expertise differs from software development. She stresses that considerable effort and difficult transition periods should be anticipated rather than surprising firms.

kp.k: Fixed fees may reshape mid-market firm economics
kp.d: In the forward-looking discussion, Buckley says mid-sized firms are not discussing commercial-model change enough. She reports hearing from some firms that clients only want to pay for seniors, not juniors; this is client sentiment relayed through firms and the vendor, not a measured market-wide finding. She predicts further growth in project-level and fixed-fee pricing focused on output rather than rates attached to individuals, and recommends planning for the consequences for firm economics. She remains broadly optimistic about firms’ adaptability and expects firms with strong client relationships and organised data to fare better.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Buckley argues that AI shifts work toward verification and makes integrated workflows, institutional knowledge, training, client relationships and pricing reform increasingly important.
pts.d: At 04:50, Triona Buckley argues that accelerating drafting shifts responsibility upstream to more expensive people who must check research, thoughtfulness and citations. She advocates connecting tasks through agentic AI and addressing administrative friction and information silos rather than optimizing isolated tasks. At 08:05–10:47, she says capturing actions and reasons during ordinary work can build institutional knowledge, while connected data supplies AI with context and an audit trail records human and agent activity. At 13:30–16:52, she argues that AI tutors grounded in firm knowledge can prompt deeper questions and appropriate checking, standardize otherwise inconsistent informal training and accelerate junior lawyers’ development. At 18:12–18:36, she identifies a transitional workload bottleneck: staff must pursue AI returns while maintaining their existing responsibilities and handling implementation issues. At 20:31–22:35, she says Trace uses AI and work context to link activity to matters and present readily confirmable time entries, recovering previously unrecorded billable work; better time data also supports quoting, pricing, utilization and bottleneck identification. At 24:27, she argues that mid-market firms can be especially well positioned for AI because they tend to have fewer tools, can change more readily when professionally managed, and already emphasize senior-level client relationships. She predicts that nuanced advisory relationships will become more important relative to document quality. At 34:37, she predicts stronger outcomes for firms investing in relationships and organized data, and more project-level and fixed-fee pricing focused on outputs rather than individual hourly rates.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Buckley relies principally on law-firm experience, customer observations and feedback from implementation partners; projected benefits are not accompanied by quantified evaluation results.
pts.d: Buckley identifies her day-to-day customer work and previous experience inside law firms as the basis for her account of workflows, resources and informal training. She reports seeing a few innovative firms recognize AI’s training potential, but supplies no named case study or measured learning outcome. Her time-capture claims draw on reported customer use of Actionstep’s Trace product and asserted gains. The example of recovering 30 additional minutes a day is conditional, not a reported sample average or measured effect. No sample sizes, baseline comparisons, collection rates, implementation costs or quantified ROI calculation are supplied. Her account of changing client expectations includes reports from some firms that clients want to pay for seniors rather than juniors. She also says she draws market insights from customers and advisory partners working with firms. Her comparative claims about mid-market readiness and predictions about relationships and pricing are reasoned professional judgments, not presented as results of a comparative AI study. The tool-sprawl percentages and the tutoring-percentile assertion in the transcript are introduced by the host, not established by Buckley as her own evidence.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Buckley distinguishes current adoption and product use from prospective benefits, with successful adoption conditional on connected data, governance, management capacity and planned change.
pts.d: The interview is presented as a 2026 source. Buckley describes drafting tools, emerging agentic workflow opportunities, early interest in AI tutoring and Trace customer use as current developments. She says the first Trace version is already in market and another version covering more tools is due the following month; no calendar date is supplied. Her broader commercial predictions concern the coming AI transition without an independently specified deadline. Institutional-knowledge capture must occur within ordinary work rather than require a separate effort, and governance must preserve who did what, when and why. AI requires connected information, but she explicitly qualifies that this need not mean a single platform. AI tutoring is intended to augment, not replace, formal training and senior–junior interaction. The mid-market change-management advantage is particularly associated with firms that have invested in strong professional management. Technology adoption requires planning around actual processes, identifying bottlenecks and appointing champions; she frames these projects in months rather than weeks and acknowledges substantial implementation effort. More accurate time records remain relevant to understanding profitability even as firms move toward fixed fees.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The central constituency is mid-market law firms, with distinct implications for senior lawyers, juniors, fee earners, management, support teams and clients.
pts.d: Senior lawyers face upstream verification demands from faster drafting, while system-level automation is intended to free fee earners for client judgment. Junior lawyers are potential beneficiaries of more consistent, firm-specific tutoring rather than being described by Buckley as a class destined for elimination. Mid-market firms, which usually lack the knowledge and innovation teams of larger firms, could capture expertise within daily workflows and use AI-supported training to compete with larger firms. Their partners and other lawyers may gain competitive value from close advisory relationships. Trainers, IT staff and others responsible for adoption face additional work alongside their existing jobs. Fee earners using passive time capture may record more work already performed; management gains information for utilization, quoting, profitability analysis and process improvement. Clients are described as increasingly questioning payment for junior work and as potential buyers of more output-focused, fixed-fee engagements. Actionstep is the software vendor whose product strategy Buckley discusses, not a provider delivering legal work. The discussion concerns law-firm operations and commercial services, not a claim about access to justice or measured profession-wide employment displacement.
